description: What UX is, good vs faulty design, users and stakeholders

screens.body:
UX — user experience — is the WHOLE experience of using something: how it feels, how easy it is, whether it respects your time. It's not "making it pretty." Pretty is UI. UX is whether the thing actually works for the human holding it.

Every app you love has good UX hiding underneath: you never notice it, because nothing confused you, nothing wasted your time, nothing made you feel dumb. Good UX is invisible.

options: The whole experience of using something — ease, feeling, respect for your time
Just making screens pretty
The code behind the app
check.question: UX is…

screens.heading: It's not just pretty screens
screens.keyPoint: Good UX is invisible; you only notice bad UX.

screens.body:
Good design is forgiving and clear: buttons say what they do, mistakes are easy to undo, and the next step is obvious. Faulty design does the opposite — it confuses, punishes, and blames the user.

The classic example: a door with a handle you pull, but the sign says PUSH. You pull it — everyone does — and feel silly. That's not your fault; it's faulty design. The door failed YOU. Software does this constantly: tiny grey text, destructive buttons next to safe ones, error messages that say "Error 0x4F" and nothing else.

options: Clear, forgiving, obvious next steps — and faulty design blames the user for its own failures
Expensive-looking visuals
Lots of features on one screen
check.question: Good design is…

screens.heading: Good design vs faulty design
screens.keyPoint: When users fail, the design failed first.

screens.body:
In UX, a "user" is simply the person using what you build — and defining them precisely is half the job. "Everyone" is not a user. "A SAIT student booking a braid appointment between classes" is a user.

Different users bring different needs, abilities, and contexts: a first-time visitor vs a daily power user, someone on a cracked phone screen in bright sunlight vs someone on a laptop. Design for a real someone, not an abstract everyone.

options: The specific person using the product — defined precisely, not "everyone"
Only the person who pays
The developer
check.question: A user is…

screens.heading: Who exactly is the user?

screens.body:
Stakeholders are everyone with a stake in the outcome: users, the client paying for it, developers building it, support staff answering for it, the business chasing revenue. Their needs genuinely clash — the business wants sign-ups; users want to skip sign-up.

Your job isn't to please everyone. It's to surface the conflicts early and make deliberate tradeoffs — ideally in favor of the user, since they're the ones who decide whether the thing lives or dies.

options: Everyone with a stake: users, client, devs, business — with needs that can clash
Only the investors
Only the design team
check.question: Stakeholders are…

screens.heading: Everyone with a stake
screens.keyPoint: Surface conflicts early; usually side with the user.

screens.body:
The UX process is a loop, not a straight line: understand the problem → design a solution → test it with users → learn → repeat. You never get it right the first time, and that's the plan, not a failure.

Problem analysis comes first — before any screens. If you solve the wrong problem beautifully, you've built a polished irrelevance. Fall in love with the problem, not your first solution.

options: Understand → design → test → repeat, starting with problem analysis
Design screens first, ask questions later
Build it once, perfectly
check.question: The UX process is…

screens.heading: The loop: understand, design, test
screens.keyPoint: Fall in love with the problem, not the solution.

screens.body:
Because it's a loop, you need milestones — checkpoints where you stop and ask "are we on the right track?" A tested wireframe, a round of user feedback, a prototype review. Each milestone is a chance to catch a wrong turn while it's still cheap.

Continuous feedback is the fuel: show work early and often, to users AND stakeholders. Feedback on a sketch costs a conversation; feedback on a finished app costs a rebuild.

options: Checkpoints with user and stakeholder feedback to catch wrong turns early
One big reveal at the end
Avoiding feedback so it doesn't slow you down
check.question: Milestones and feedback exist to…

screens.heading: Checkpoints, not cliffhangers
screens.keyPoint: Show work early; feedback is cheapest on sketches.

screens.body:
Here's the relationship that matters: users don't just receive the design — they SHAPE it. Their behavior in tests, their complaints, their workarounds: that's the design brief talking back.

The best UX designers stay curious about users instead of defensive about designs. Every "your app is confusing" is a gift — it's a user doing your research for free.

options: Users shape the design through feedback, tests, and behavior
Users just receive whatever is built
Designers should defend their work from users
check.question: Users and the design process:

screens.heading: Users are co-designers

screens.body: Nielsen Norman Group (nngroup.com) — the research firm founded by usability pioneers; the definitive source on UX principles. W3C (w3.org) — web standards including accessibility, which is UX for everyone. Google's Material Design (material.io) — a full official design system to study real standards in action.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: NNG is the gold standard for UX research.
